# Building 4410: Division 26 project specifications (final submittal)

You are the electrical Designer of Record at Harlan Sato Engineers LLC, the architect-engineer for the new Company
Operations Facility, Building 4410, at Fort Calder, an Army design-bid-build project. The electrical design is
complete and coordinated in a building information model. Your task order is to produce the **Division 26 project
specifications** that tell the general contractor and the electrical contractor what to buy and how to install and
test it, edited from the Unified Facilities Guide Specifications to this project's criteria, owner requirements and
installation standard, together with the electrical design basis the specifications rest on.

The project documents are in this workspace: the A/E scope of work and design directives, the transmittal log and
design review comments, the Owner's Project Requirements, the installation electrical design standard, the drawings
and schedules, the electrical coordination model, the utility service data, the calculation basis memoranda, product
data and photometric files, the governing criteria and federal regulations, and the guide specification library. Some
folders hold superseded revisions or material from other agencies; the scope of work and the transmittal log say what
is current and what governs. The NFPA 70 text is not provided.

## What to deliver

`output/submission.zip` containing:

1. `specs/`: **one `.docx` per Division 26 section this task order delivers**, numbered and titled as the
   corresponding Unified Facilities Guide Specification, each a finished project section tailored from that guide
   specification. Edit the guide specification rather than writing sections from scratch: a document that does not
   retain the guide specification's text is not treated as a project section. The scope of work says which sections
   this task order delivers; sections delivered under another task order are neither required nor penalised.
2. `design_basis.xlsx`: the electrical design basis workbook, with these sheets (header in row 1, one record per
   row; extra columns are ignored):

| sheet | columns |
|---|---|
| `Sections` | `number`, `title`, `basis` (why the section is in the project) |
| `Feeders` | `feeder`, `route_length_ft`, `sets`, `size`, `raceway_in`, `vd_pct`, `fill_pct`: one row per feeder and service run on the one-line diagram |
| `ShortCircuit` | `bus`, `voltage_v`, `available_fault_ka`, `specified_rating_ka`: one row per switchboard, panelboard and transfer switch bus on the one-line diagram |
| `Photometric` | `space`, `luminaire_type`, `quantity`, `avg_maintained_fc`, `min_fc`, `uniformity`, `lpd_w_ft2`: one row per interior space in the coordination model |
| `StepLoad` | `step`, `loads`, `step_kva_start`, `voltage_dip_pct`, `recovery_s`: one row per load step, in the order the loads are placed on the engine-generator |
| `Register` | `req_id`, `document` (number/title, with revision or change where there are several), `clause` (paragraph, table, note or row), `requirement`, `value` (the governing number or choice), `applies_to` (section numbers) |
| `Findings` | `finding_id`, `document`, `location`, `defect`, `correction`: errors or inconsistencies you found in the furnished documents and how you resolved them |

## Section format

Each section document must read, as plain paragraphs of text:

- `SECTION nn nn nn` (the section number), the section title, and the section date line;
- `PART 1   GENERAL`, `PART 2   PRODUCTS`, `PART 3   EXECUTION` (a part without content reads `Not used.`);
- articles numbered as typed text, `1.1 REFERENCES`, `1.2 ...`, with upper-case titles; lower-level paragraphs
  `1.2.1 Title`; list items `a.`, `(1)`, `(a)`, `1.`;
- `-- End of Section --` as the last paragraph.

Numbering, list markers and section headings must be literal text in the paragraphs; automatic Word list numbering is
not read. Only paragraph text is read (tables in a section are read cell by cell as paragraphs). Any tool that writes a
valid `.docx` (WordprocessingML package) is fine; no word processor is installed in this workspace, and a `.docx` can be
written with the Python standard library (`zipfile` plus the three required parts: `[Content_Types].xml`, `_rels/.rels`,
`word/document.xml`). No BIM or photometric toolkit is installed either; the coordination model and the photometric
files are text formats and can be parsed with the standard library.

## How the package is judged

Each delivered section is judged as one item against requirements recomputed from the project documents,
independently of wording; values are compared after unit conversion. The design-basis sheets are judged by re-running
the calculations against the design you declare, and the numbers you report are checked against that re-run. A section
with an unresolved choice, or whose design is unsafe or unbuildable, fails a hard requirement family.
Specifications are performance-based and must not be more restrictive than the governing requirement
(FAR 11.002(a)(1)(ii)); a design that meets every limit without over-providing earns the most objective credit. A hard
governing requirement that a section's design rests on and that is missing from your `Register` fails one more hard
family of that section. Each section scores `0.4·p + 0.6·[h = 1]·O`, where `p` is the weighted fraction of the section's
requirement families passed, `h` the weighted fraction of its hard families passed (`[h = 1]` is 1 when every hard
family passes, else 0), and `O` its over-specification credit: a failed hard family zeroes the `O` term.
There is no required number of rows on the `Register` and `Findings` sheets. Defects in the furnished documents and in
the furnished design are scored, so a defect you find and correct belongs on `Findings`, with the correction you made.


## Verifier access (blind variant)

No verifier, oracle, or evaluation data of any kind is available in this workspace; the
only checks you can run are the ones you build yourself. Work from the brief and the
documents alone and submit your best final deliverable; it will be graded offline by the
frozen verifier on held-out instances.

import zipfile, xml.etree.ElementTree as ET, openpyxl, os

def read_docx(path):
    print('=== DOCX:', path, '===')
    with zipfile.ZipFile(path) as z:
        xml_content = z.read('word/document.xml')
    tree = ET.fromstring(xml_content)
    for p in tree.iter('{http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/wordprocessingml/2006/main}p'):
        texts = [t.text for t in p.iter('{http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/wordprocessingml/2006/main}t') if t.text]
        if texts:
            print(''.join(texts))

def read_xlsx(path):
    print('=== XLSX:', path, '===')
    wb = openpyxl.load_workbook(path, data_only=True)
    for name in wb.sheetnames:
        print('--- Sheet:', name, '---')
        ws = wb[name]
        for row in ws.iter_rows(values_only=True):
            if any(row):
                print([str(c) if c is not None else '' for c in row])

Architect-Engineer Scope of Work — Electrical Design, Final (100 %) Submittal
Contract W912XX-27-C-0418 (PN 90417). Company Operations Facility (COF), Building 4410, Fort Calder, Georgia. U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Savannah District (fictional project).
1 GENERAL
1.1 Project. New two-story Company Operations Facility for an Army unit (Army project, new construction; no renovation). The facility is on an inland installation in Georgia; no state or local electrical amendments apply on the installation.
1.2 Delivery method. Design-bid-build. The A/E is the Designer of Record (DOR) and prepares the construction contract documents: drawings, specifications and the design analysis.
1.3 Scope of this task order. Prepare the Division 26 project specification sections listed in 3.9, and the electrical design basis workbook, for the final (100 %) submittal.
Table 1 — Electrical systems inventory (1.3). Present: main switchboard MSB; 480 V panelboards HM1, H1A, H2A, HE1; dry-type transformers T-1A, T-2A, T-C1, T-E1; 208 V panelboards LP1A, LP2A, LC1, LE1; engine-generator GEN-1; automatic transfer switches ATS-L (Article 700, bypass-isolation) and ATS-E (Article 702); advanced meter; SPDs at MSB and LC1; grounding electrode system with ground ring; lightning protection system; interior and exterior LED lighting; variable frequency drives on AHU-1 and AHU-2 (furnished under Division 23). Not in this project: busway; power cable tray; motor control centers; lighting control panelboards / relay panels; residential load centers; hazardous (classified) locations; 400 Hz systems; 270 V dc systems; medium-voltage work (utility furnishes primary); UPS (owner-furnished rack units only); photovoltaic system; paralleling switchgear; fire pump. Water service: HDPE (nonmetallic). Service entrance: underground, six 4 in PVC Schedule 40 ducts, concrete-encased, from the utility pad-mounted transformer to MSB; the secondary service conductors are sized by the Designer of Record in the design basis (3.4), and the conductors shown on E-601 Rev C are the 35 % submittal selection.
1.3.1 Government-furnished electrical coordination model. The Government furnishes, with the contract drawings, the electrical coordination model 50_bim/BLDG4410-E_RevC.ifc, an IFC4 (ISO 16739-1) model of the building authored in millimetres. The model is a contract document. It carries the building spaces and their dimensions, the electrical equipment locations, the interior luminaires of each space, and the routed feeder raceways, each raceway run identified by the feeder tag it carries. Dimensions, luminaire quantities and locations, routed feeder lengths and raceway trade sizes are taken from the model: they are not dimensioned or scheduled on the drawings. Also furnished are the LM-63 photometric files of the scheduled interior luminaire types, in 40_product_data/photometrics.
1.4 Schedule. Construction award April 2027; electrical equipment deliveries (switchboard, dry-type transformers, generator, transfer switch) June 2028; beneficial occupancy March 2029.
1.5 Order of precedence. Where requirements of the following documents differ, the order of precedence is: (1) this SOW; (2) Unified Facilities Criteria and federal regulations; (3) the installation standard IES-26; (4) the Owner's Project Requirements (current revision). A lower-precedence document may add or tighten a requirement; the more stringent requirement then governs unless the higher-precedence document prohibits it. Superseded revisions have no standing. Use only the current revisions listed in the transmittal log.
2 CRITERIA
2.1 Design to UFC 1-200-01, UFC 3-501-01, UFC 3-520-01 (current change), the federal regulations in the criteria folder, IES-26 and the OPR. NFPA 70 (edition adopted by UFC 1-200-01) applies but is not furnished. UFC 1-200-02 high performance and sustainable building requirements apply; no third-party certification is sought.
2.2 Use the Unified Facilities Guide Specifications (UFGS) Division 26 masters furnished in the guide specification library (August 2026 update). Other agencies' master specifications in the library are for reference only and must not be used as project specification text.
3 SPECIFICATION REQUIREMENTS
3.1 Tailoring. Tailor each UFGS for an Army design-bid-build project: keep only the Army tailoring options, resolve every bracketed choice and blank, delete notes to the specifier, and delete requirements for equipment and systems the project does not have.
3.2 Photometrics. The DOR provides the photometric calculations in the design analysis; the specifications must not require the Contractor to prepare photometric plans.
3.3 Format. UFS 1-300-02 is incorporated into this SOW and is binding for the project specifications regardless of its For-Information-Only status. English (inch-pound) units only. Deliver each section as a separate DOCX document (the Government converts them to Google Docs for review).
3.4 Ratings and delegated design. The panelboard and switchboard schedules on the drawings do not show short-circuit current ratings: state the minimum short-circuit current rating of the switchboard and of the 480 V and 208 V panelboards in the specifications, from the short-circuit study basis SCB-01 method and the current utility data. Seismic restraint of electrical equipment is a Contractor delegated design by a registered professional engineer; the DOR reviews it.
3.5 Power system studies. The Contractor performs the short-circuit, protective device coordination and arc flash studies on as-built data in accordance with Section 26 05 73 and provides device settings; the DOR reviews them. Electronic-trip breakers are used to achieve selective coordination. The studies are construction-phase studies for protective device settings and arc flash labels; scope: from the utility transformer secondary through every 480 V and 208 V bus (MSB, HM1, H1A, H2A, ATS-E, HE1, ATS-L, LP1A, LP2A, LC1, LE1), for the normal and the generator source, using the utility data of UP-4410 Rev 2. The study engineer is a registered professional engineer with 5 years of power system study experience and seals the studies.

Owner's Project Requirements (OPR) — Building 4410, Revision B
Company Operations Facility (COF), Building 4410, Fort Calder, Georgia. Prepared by Fort Calder Directorate of Public Works for the using unit. Revision B, 30 June 2026.
1 Project description
Two-story company operations facility: administrative offices, company storage, a training room (Room 140), a staff duty desk (Room 101) and a communications room (Room 116).
4 Environmental and operating requirements
4.3 Electrical rooms are conditioned; maximum 85 F.
5 Electrical systems
5.1 Conductors: copper for all feeders and branch circuits.
5.2 Switchboard: provide energy-reducing maintenance switching with local status indicator as the arc energy reduction method for the main breaker.
5.3 Dry-type transformers: meet the 10 CFR 431.196(a)(3) efficiency levels that apply to units manufactured on or after April 23, 2029, regardless of the manufacture date. Additional overload capacity is required for the communications transformer T-C1 (nonlinear electronic loads); no additional overload capacity is required for the other transformers. T-C1 is adjacent to the communications room, a noise-sensitive space.
5.4 Communications Room 116 houses sensitive electronic equipment: provide cascaded surge protection at panelboard LC1 in addition to the service entrance, and a building ground ring.
5.5 Standby power: on-site fuel for 96 hours at full load in the generator sub-base tank; outdoor sound-attenuated aluminum enclosure; bypass-isolation automatic transfer arrangement for the life-safety transfer switch ATS-L so it can be maintained without an outage; remote annunciator at the Staff Duty desk, Room 101.
5.6 Lighting: interior 3500 K; no color-critical visual tasks; standard catalogue luminaires (no samples); Training Room 140 uses the standard dimming range (no presentation dimming); egress and exit lighting on the generator life-safety branch.
5.7 Lightning protection is required.
6 Operation, maintenance and warranty
6.1 Acceptance testing by an independent NETA-accredited testing organization to NETA ATS.
6.2 Extended warranties (approved by the Contracting Officer, memorandum CO-4410-07): engine-generator set 5 years; automatic transfer switch 5 years; surge protective devices 5 years; LED luminaires 10 years; lighting poles 3 years.
6.3 Training: switchboard 4 hours; engine-generator set 8 hours; transfer switch 4 hours; lighting controls 4 hours.
7 Revision history
Rev B: conductor material changed to copper throughout; transformer requirements revised (efficiency basis, overload capacity for T-C1 only); fuel storage increased to 96 hours; interior CCT 3500 K; warranty periods updated; the 5-ohm grounding value of Rev A is withdrawn — grounding electrode system resistance is governed by IES-26.

1 General

recorded ambient 38 C; heating design dry bulb (99.6 %) 18 F (-8 C).
1.5 The electrical coordination model issued with the contract drawings (50_bim/BLDG4410-E_RevC.ifc) is a contract
document of equal standing with the drawings. Dimensions, equipment and luminaire locations, luminaire quantities
and routed raceway lengths are taken from that model; they are not dimensioned or scheduled on the drawings.
Where the model and a drawing disagree, report the discrepancy to the Contracting Officer before proceeding.
4 Wiring
4.1 Copper conductors only. 4.2 Insulation: feeders XHHW-2; branch circuits THHN/THWN-2.
4.3 Phase identification: 480Y/277 V brown, orange, yellow, neutral gray; 208Y/120 V black, red, blue, neutral white.
4.4 Metal-clad (MC) and armored (AC) cable are not permitted in new buildings.
4.5 Raceways: EMT concealed and above ceilings; RMC exposed below 8 ft in mechanical and electrical rooms and
exposed on building exteriors; PVC Schedule 40 underground and in slabs, with RMC or PVC-coated RMC elbows
and risers; liquidtight flexible metal conduit for final connections to vibrating equipment, 6 ft maximum. ENT, LFNC
and surface nonmetallic raceway are not permitted.
4.6 Raceway fill. Where more than two conductors are installed in one raceway, the sum of the overall cross-sectional
areas of the conductors must not exceed 40 percent of the interior cross-sectional area of the raceway. Take the
conductor overall areas from the project conductor data sheet CDS-7 and the raceway interior areas from the project
raceway data sheet RDS-1; the corresponding tables of NFPA 70 Chapter 9 are not reproduced in this standard and
are cited by designation only. Install each parallel conductor set of a feeder in its own raceway; a feeder run must not
carry more parallel sets than it has raceways. Count, in each raceway, three phase conductors, one neutral of the
same size as the phase conductors, and one equipment grounding conductor. Size the equipment grounding
conductor of a feeder the same size as the phase conductor where the phase conductor is smaller than 250 kcmil,
and one size smaller than the phase conductor in the CDS-7 size list where the phase conductor is 250 kcmil or
larger. Where a phase conductor is increased in size for voltage drop, increase the equipment grounding conductor
by the same rule.
4.7 Voltage drop. UFC 3-501-01 paragraph 3-2.7.1 governs and is adopted without change: 3 percent maximum for
feeders and service conductors, 3 percent maximum for branch circuits, and 5 percent maximum total from the point
of Government ownership to the furthest outlet. In addition, and more stringently, limit the voltage drop of any feeder
of the emergency system to 2 percent of nominal voltage. A feeder is a feeder of the emergency system when it
carries emergency system load, that is: the feeder from the normal source to the emergency system transfer switch;
the feeder from the alternate (engine-generator) source to that same transfer switch; and every feeder on the load
side of that transfer switch, including the primary and secondary feeders of any transformer serving emergency
system load. The emergency system transfer switch is the transfer switch shown on the one-line diagram as serving
NFPA 70 Article 700 loads. Feeders serving only optional standby (NFPA 70 Article 702) load are not feeders of the
emergency system and keep the UFC allowance, as do the service conductors, which are not feeders. Calculate

import fitz, openpyxl

def read_pdf(path):
    print('=== PDF:', path, '===')
    doc = fitz.open(path)
    for i, page in enumerate(doc):
        print(f'--- Page {i+1} ---')
        print(page.get_text())

def read_xlsx(path, sheets=None):
    print('=== XLSX:', path, '===')
    wb = openpyxl.load_workbook(path, data_only=True)
    for name in (sheets or wb.sheetnames):
        print('--- Sheet:', name, '---')
        ws = wb[name]
        for row in ws.iter_rows(values_only=True):
            if any(row):
                print([str(c) if c is not None else '' for c in row])

base = '/filesystem/final_batch4__electrical_task8_electrical_specs__blind'

FDB-01 Feeder Design Basis — Building 4410 (Rev 1)
Harlan Sato Engineers LLC (A/E, Designer of Record). Establishes the method by which every feeder of Building
4410 is sized. This memorandum states the method and the input data only; it states no result. The conductor size,
the number of parallel sets and, where required, the corrected raceway size for each feeder are developed in the
electrical design basis workbook.
1. Scope and governing criteria
Every feeder listed in Table 1 is sized to satisfy all three of the following simultaneously: (a) allowable ampacity not
less than the design load; (b) voltage drop not more than the allowance of the installation electrical design standard
IES-26 paragraph 4.7, which adopts UFC 3-501-01 paragraph 3-2.7.1 and tightens the feeders of the emergency
system; and (c) raceway fill not more than the limit of IES-26 paragraph 4.6. Conductors are copper throughout (OPR
paragraph 5.1, IES-26 paragraph 4.1), 75 C rated, with 75 C terminations. Conductor properties are from conductor
data sheet CDS-7; raceway interior areas are from raceway data sheet RDS-1.
2. Feeder design load and geometry
The design load of each feeder is given in Table 1. For a feeder to a panelboard it is the connected load of the panel
schedule on drawing E-701 with the demand factors of the generator and load calculation GLC-01; for a transformer
primary feeder it is the load corresponding to the nominal output rating of the transformer; for a feeder to a transfer
switch it is the load transferred by that switch.
The one-way routed length of each feeder, and the trade size and number of raceways in each feeder run, are NOT
stated on the drawings. They are taken from the electrical coordination model 50_bim/BLDG4410-E_RevC.ifc, in
which each raceway run carries the feeder tag of Table 1 as its reference property. Take the one-way routed length
as the total developed length of the routed raceway run of that feeder, including the vertical rises and drops,
measured along the centre line of the raceway from the source termination to the load termination. Do not use a
straight-line distance and do not use the raceways of any other system or of a superseded revision.

3. Voltage drop
Calculate the line-to-line voltage drop of a three-phase feeder as
    VD (volts) = sqrt(3) x I x (R x cos(theta) + X x sin(theta)) x L / 1000 / N
in which I is the design load of Table 1 in amperes; R and X are the alternating-current resistance at 75 C and the
reactance, in ohms per 1000 feet, of one conductor of the selected size, read from conductor data sheet CDS-7; L is
the one-way routed length in feet taken from the coordination model as described in paragraph 2; and N is the
number of parallel conductor sets.
The design power factor is 0.9 lagging for every feeder, so cos(theta) = 0.9 and sin(theta) = sqrt(1 - 0.9 x 0.9) =
0.4359. Do not use a different power factor for individual feeders.
Express the voltage drop as a percentage of the nominal line-to-line voltage of Table 1: VD (per cent) = 100 x VD
(volts) / V(nominal). Compare that percentage with the allowance of IES-26 paragraph 4.7 for the feeder concerned.
Each feeder is evaluated over its own length only; the cumulative check against the total allowance is made
separately in the design basis workbook.
4. Raceway fill
Each parallel conductor set occupies one raceway of the feeder run. A feeder run therefore cannot carry more parallel
sets than it has raceways; a design with more sets than the modelled run has raceways is infeasible and must be
rejected.
Each set consists of five conductors: three phase conductors, one full-size neutral of the same size as the phase
conductors, and one equipment grounding conductor. Size the equipment grounding conductor by the rule of IES-26
paragraph 4.6: the same size as the phase conductor where the phase conductor is smaller than 250 kcmil, and one
size smaller than the phase conductor in the CDS-7 size list where the phase conductor is 250 kcmil or larger.
The area occupied in one raceway is therefore
    A(occupied) = 4 x A(phase conductor) + 1 x A(equipment grounding conductor)
using the overall areas of column 4 of CDS-7. The percentage fill of that raceway is 100 x A(occupied) / A(interior), in
which A(interior) is the interior cross-sectional area of the raceway, read from raceway data sheet RDS-1 for the
raceway material of Table 1 and the trade size shown in the coordination model. The limit is the percentage of IES-26
paragraph 4.6.

--- Page 3 ---
FDB-01 Rev 1
Harlan Sato Engineers LLC (A/E, Designer of Record)   Page 3
For the feeders routed in the underground duct bank, the conduit fill and the jam ratio are also submittal items under
Section 33 71 02 paragraph 3.3; the fill computed by this paragraph is the value to be reported.
5. Ampacity
The allowable ampacity of the feeder is N x (the 75 C ampacity of one conductor of the selected size, column 5 of
CDS-7), in which N is the number of parallel sets. The allowable ampacity must not be less than the design load of
Table 1. Terminations are rated 75 C throughout, so the 75 C column governs at every termination.
6. The coordination model governs the raceway size
The raceway trade size shown in the coordination model is the size of the installed raceway and it governs the fill
calculation. Where no conductor in the CDS-7 catalogue, in any permitted number of parallel sets, can satisfy
ampacity, voltage drop and raceway fill simultaneously in the raceway the model shows, the model is in error. In that
case record the discrepancy as a finding against the coordination model and state, as part of the finding, the raceway
trade size the design requires: the smallest trade size of the same raceway material in which a compliant conductor
selection exists. Do not silently exceed the fill limit, do not relax the voltage drop allowance, and do not assume a
raceway size that the model does not show unless the finding is recorded.
7. Data sources
Conductor resistance, reactance, overall area and 75 C ampacity: CDS-7. Raceway interior area: RDS-1. Raceway
material by feeder: Table 1 of this memorandum, which follows IES-26 paragraph 4.5. Routed length, raceway trade
size and number of raceways per run: the coordination model 50_bim/BLDG4410-E_RevC.ifc. Design load: Table 1
of this memorandum, from E-701 and GLC-01. Voltage drop allowances: IES-26 paragraph 4.7 and UFC 3-501-01
paragraph 3-2.7.1. Raceway fill limit and equipment grounding conductor sizing: IES-26 paragraph 4.6.

--- Page 1 ---
GSB-01 Rev 1
Harlan Sato Engineers LLC (A/E, Designer of Record)   Page 1
GSB-01 Generator Step-Load Basis — Building 4410 (Rev 1)
Harlan Sato Engineers LLC (A/E, Designer of Record). Establishes the method by which the sequence in which load
is placed on the standby engine-generator GEN-1 is developed and verified. This memorandum states the method
and the input data only; it states no transient voltage dip, no recovery time and no step sequence.
1. Scope
On loss of the normal source the engine-generator starts and the transfer switches transfer their loads to it. The load
is not placed on the set all at once: it is placed in steps. The step-load sequence is a design deliverable. Each step is
a group of load tags placed on the set at the same instant; the steps are taken in order, the set recovering to steady
state between steps.
2. Load data
The loads that transfer to the engine-generator, the running kVA and the starting (locked-rotor) kVA of each, and the
transfer switch that serves each, are scheduled on the mechanical equipment schedule M-601 (sheet 'Generator
transfer loads') and, for the motor-driven equipment, in the nameplate data of sheet 'M-601'. Machine data for the set
are on the manufacturer's data sheet GEN-1. Acceptance limits are in the installation electrical design standard
IES-26 paragraph 10.7.
3. Transient voltage dip of a step
Calculate the transient voltage dip caused by one step as
    dip (per cent) = 100 x Xd2 x kVA(step) / ( kVA(alternator) + Xd2 x ( kVA(step) + kVA(running) ) )
in which Xd2 is the saturated direct-axis subtransient reactance of the alternator in per unit on its own kVA base, from
data sheet GEN-1 (0.12 per unit); kVA(alternator) is the standby kVA rating of the set from data sheet GEN-1 (187.5
kVA); kVA(step) is the sum of the starting (locked-rotor) kVA of every load tag added at that step; and kVA(running) is
the sum of the running kVA of every load tag already carried by the set immediately before that step. For the first step
kVA(running) is zero.
A load that is not motor-driven has a starting kVA equal to its running kVA, as scheduled. Use the scheduled
locked-rotor kVA as it is; do not apply a starting-current multiplier of your own and do not apply a reduced-voltage
starting credit, since no unit is scheduled with a reduced-voltage starter.
4. Recovery time of a step
Take the time for the set to recover from a step as
    t(recovery, seconds) = 0.6 + 0.08 x dip (per cent)
using the dip of paragraph 3 for that step, expressed in per cent. The recovery time of every step must satisfy the limit
of IES-26 paragraph 10.7.
5. Rules the sequence must satisfy
a. Every load that transfers to the engine-generator must appear in the sequence exactly once. A load may not be
started twice and no load may be omitted.
b. Every load of the emergency system, that is every load served by the emergency (life safety) transfer switch, which
is the transfer switch identified on E-601 as serving NFPA 70 Article 700 loads, must be carried by the first step. The
emergency transfer switch restores its loads within 10 seconds of loss of the normal source (IES-26 paragraph 10.6),

--- Page 2 ---
GSB-01 Rev 1
Harlan Sato Engineers LLC (A/E, Designer of Record)   Page 2
so its loads cannot wait for a later step. Optional standby loads may be placed on any step.
c. The transient voltage dip of every step must not exceed the limit of IES-26 paragraph 10.7.
d. The total running load carried by the set when every load has transferred, taken as the sum of the running kVA of
all transferred loads multiplied by the rated power factor of the set from data sheet GEN-1 (0.8), must not exceed the
standby kilowatt rating of the set (150 kW).
e. A step may not be empty.
6. Deliverable
State the sequence as an ordered list of steps, each step being the list of load tags of M-601 placed on the set at that
step. Report, for each step, the summed starting kVA, the running kVA carried before the step, the transient voltage
dip and the recovery time. Any sequence that satisfies paragraph 5 is acceptable; where the number of steps is an
objective, the fewest steps that satisfy paragraph 5 is the target.

PCB-01 Photometric Calculation Basis — Building 4410 (Rev 1)
Harlan Sato Engineers LLC (A/E, Designer of Record). Establishes the method by which the interior illuminance of
every space of Building 4410 is calculated and by which a luminaire quantity is verified. This memorandum states the
method and the input data only; it states no calculated illuminance, uniformity, lighting power density or luminaire
quantity.
1. Governing criteria
Section 26 51 00 requires computer-generated photometric plans for each space, using the applicable light loss
factor, to verify that the proposed luminaires and locations meet the required performance criteria. That section
establishes, for the calculation: horizontal illuminance taken at a maximum of every one foot (305 mm) across the
task area; a recommended light loss factor of 0.81 for LED luminaires; uniformity calculated as the ratio of the
average calculated illuminance over the minimum calculated illuminance of the calculation grid; and a 10 percent
margin of error on each target, a 'Minimum Average' being an average taken over the entire task area that may not be
less than the stated value within that margin.
The target illumination levels for each interior application, in the 'Minimum Average' and 'Uniformity' vocabulary of that
section, are given in the installation electrical design standard IES-26 paragraph 11.6. The whole-building interior
lighting power density limit is IES-26 paragraph 11.7. Surface reflectances are scheduled on A-601. Room
dimensions, ceiling heights, luminaire positions and luminaire quantities are taken from the electrical coordination
model 50_bim/BLDG4410-E_RevC.ifc.
The light loss factor used for every LED luminaire in this project is 0.81. The margin of error applied to each target is
10 percent: a calculated average maintained illuminance is acceptable when it is not less than 0.9 times the Minimum
Average of IES-26 paragraph 11.6, and a calculated uniformity is acceptable when it is not more than 1.1 times the
Uniformity limit of that paragraph.
2. Luminous flux of a luminaire: zonal integration of the candela table
Each interior luminaire type is described by an LM-63 photometric file named in the luminaire schedule E-501 and
issued in 40_product_data/photometrics/. The candela table of that file gives, for each horizontal angle present in the
file, the luminous intensity in candelas at the vertical angles 0 to 90 degrees from nadir in 5 degree steps.
The luminous flux of the luminaire to be used in this calculation is the flux obtained by integrating that candela table. It
is NOT the rated lamp lumens written in the file header and it is NOT the rated lamp lumens scheduled on E-501;
those are lamp values and are larger than the flux the luminaire emits. Obtain the flux as follows.
a. For each vertical angle in the table, form the mean intensity over the horizontal angles. Where the file contains a
single horizontal plane, the mean is that plane's value at that vertical angle. Where the file contains more than one
horizontal plane, take the trapezoidal average over the horizontal angles present: sum, over each adjacent pair of
horizontal angles a and b, the quantity (I(a) + I(b)) / 2 multiplied by (b - a); then divide that sum by (the last horizontal
angle minus the first horizontal angle). The files are quadrant symmetric and carry horizontal angles from 0 to 90
degrees.
b. Sum the zonal contributions over the vertical angles. For each adjacent pair of vertical angles t1 and t2, add
    2 x pi x (cos t1 - cos t2) x (Ibar(t1) + Ibar(t2)) / 2
in which Ibar is the mean intensity of step (a) at that vertical angle and the angles are in radians. The sum over all
adjacent pairs is the luminous flux of one luminaire, in lumens.
3. Intensity at an arbitrary direction: bilinear interpolation

--- Page 2 ---
PCB-01 Rev 1
Harlan Sato Engineers LLC (A/E, Designer of Record)   Page 2
The intensity at a vertical angle theta from nadir and a horizontal angle phi is interpolated bilinearly from the candela
table. Fold the horizontal angle into the range 0 to 90 degrees by quadrant symmetry: take the absolute value, reduce
modulo 180 degrees and, if the result exceeds 90 degrees, replace it by 180 degrees minus the result. Interpolate
linearly between the two bounding horizontal planes of the file, and linearly between the two bounding vertical angles
of the table (the vertical angles are evenly spaced, so the fraction is the remainder of theta divided by the step,
divided by the step). Where the file contains a single horizontal plane, no horizontal interpolation is made. The
intensity is zero at and above 90 degrees from nadir.
4. Calculation grid and work plane
The work plane is a horizontal plane 2.5 feet above the finished floor of the space. The calculation grid covers the
whole floor area of the space, which is the task area for these targets.
Grid points are spaced 1 foot apart on each horizontal axis, and the first point on each axis is 0.5 foot from the wall.
On an axis of extent E feet the number of points is therefore floor((E - 2 x 0.5) / 1) + 1, not less than one, and the
points lie at the room origin on that axis plus 0.5 plus 1 times 0, 1, 2 and so on. The grid is the full cross product of the
points of the two axes. Take the room extents and the room origin from the coordination model.
5. Direct component
Let h be the mounting height of the luminaires above the work plane: the height of the luminaire above the finished
floor of its storey, taken directly from the placement of the luminaire in the coordination model, less the work plane
height of paragraph 4. All luminaires of one space are at the same height. Where h is not positive the space cannot
be calculated by this method.
For each grid point, sum over every luminaire in the space the quantity
    I(theta, phi) x (h / d) / (d x d)
in which, writing dx and dy for the horizontal offsets from the luminaire to the grid point: d = sqrt(dx x dx + dy x dy + h
x h) is the slant distance; theta = atan(sqrt(dx x dx + dy x dy) / h) is the vertical angle from nadir; and phi = atan(|dy| /
|dx|) is the horizontal angle, measured from the long axis of the luminaire, which is the +X axis of the coordination
model for every modelled interior luminaire. Where the grid point is directly under the luminaire take phi as zero;
where dx is zero and dy is not, take phi as 90 degrees. The factor (h / d) is the cosine of the angle of incidence, so the
expression is the inverse-square-cosine illuminance in footcandles when I is in candelas and the distances are in feet.
Multiply the sum at each grid point by the light loss factor 0.81 to obtain the direct component of the maintained
illuminance at that point. The average direct component is the arithmetic mean of the direct component over all grid
points.
6. Interreflected component
The interreflected component is uniform over the space and is obtained from the flux that does not reach the work
plane directly, redistributed by the average reflectance of the room surfaces:
    E(indirect) = rho / (1 - rho) x (PHI x LLF - E(direct, average) x A(work plane)) / A(room)
in which PHI is the luminous flux of one luminaire from paragraph 2 multiplied by the number of luminaires in the

average calculated illuminance over the minimum calculated illuminance of the calculation grid; and a 10 percent
margin of error on each target, a 'Minimum Average' being an average taken over the entire task area that may not be
less than the stated value within that margin.
The target illumination levels for each interior application, in the 'Minimum Average' and 'Uniformity' vocabulary of that
section, are given in the installation electrical design standard IES-26 paragraph 11.6. The whole-building interior
lighting power density limit is IES-26 paragraph 11.7. Surface reflectances are scheduled on A-601. Room
dimensions, ceiling heights, luminaire positions and luminaire quantities are taken from the electrical coordination
model 50_bim/BLDG4410-E_RevC.ifc.
The light loss factor used for every LED luminaire in this project is 0.81. The margin of error applied to each target is
10 percent: a calculated average maintained illuminance is acceptable when it is not less than 0.9 times the Minimum
Average of IES-26 paragraph 11.6, and a calculated uniformity is acceptable when it is not more than 1.1 times the
Uniformity limit of that paragraph.
2. Luminous flux of a luminaire: zonal integration of the candela table
Each interior luminaire type is described by an LM-63 photometric file named in the luminaire schedule E-501 and
issued in 40_product_data/photometrics/. The candela table of that file gives, for each horizontal angle present in the
file, the luminous intensity in candelas at the vertical angles 0 to 90 degrees from nadir in 5 degree steps.
The luminous flux of the luminaire to be used in this calculation is the flux obtained by integrating that candela table. It
is NOT the rated lamp lumens written in the file header and it is NOT the rated lamp lumens scheduled on E-501;
those are lamp values and are larger than the flux the luminaire emits. Obtain the flux as follows.
a. For each vertical angle in the table, form the mean intensity over the horizontal angles. Where the file contains a
single horizontal plane, the mean is that plane's value at that vertical angle. Where the file contains more than one
horizontal plane, take the trapezoidal average over the horizontal angles present: sum, over each adjacent pair of
horizontal angles a and b, the quantity (I(a) + I(b)) / 2 multiplied by (b - a); then divide that sum by (the last horizontal
angle minus the first horizontal angle). The files are quadrant symmetric and carry horizontal angles from 0 to 90
degrees.
b. Sum the zonal contributions over the vertical angles. For each adjacent pair of vertical angles t1 and t2, add
    2 x pi x (cos t1 - cos t2) x (Ibar(t1) + Ibar(t2)) / 2
in which Ibar is the mean intensity of step (a) at that vertical angle and the angles are in radians. The sum over all
adjacent pairs is the luminous flux of one luminaire, in lumens.
3. Intensity at an arbitrary direction: bilinear interpolation

--- Page 2 ---
PCB-01 Rev 1
Harlan Sato Engineers LLC (A/E, Designer of Record)   Page 2
The intensity at a vertical angle theta from nadir and a horizontal angle phi is interpolated bilinearly from the candela
table. Fold the horizontal angle into the range 0 to 90 degrees by quadrant symmetry: take the absolute value, reduce
modulo 180 degrees and, if the result exceeds 90 degrees, replace it by 180 degrees minus the result. Interpolate
linearly between the two bounding horizontal planes of the file, and linearly between the two bounding vertical angles
of the table (the vertical angles are evenly spaced, so the fraction is the remainder of theta divided by the step,
divided by the step). Where the file contains a single horizontal plane, no horizontal interpolation is made. The
intensity is zero at and above 90 degrees from nadir.
4. Calculation grid and work plane
The work plane is a horizontal plane 2.5 feet above the finished floor of the space. The calculation grid covers the
whole floor area of the space, which is the task area for these targets.
Grid points are spaced 1 foot apart on each horizontal axis, and the first point on each axis is 0.5 foot from the wall.
On an axis of extent E feet the number of points is therefore floor((E - 2 x 0.5) / 1) + 1, not less than one, and the
points lie at the room origin on that axis plus 0.5 plus 1 times 0, 1, 2 and so on. The grid is the full cross product of the
points of the two axes. Take the room extents and the room origin from the coordination model.
5. Direct component
Let h be the mounting height of the luminaires above the work plane: the height of the luminaire above the finished
floor of its storey, taken directly from the placement of the luminaire in the coordination model, less the work plane
height of paragraph 4. All luminaires of one space are at the same height. Where h is not positive the space cannot
be calculated by this method.
For each grid point, sum over every luminaire in the space the quantity
    I(theta, phi) x (h / d) / (d x d)
in which, writing dx and dy for the horizontal offsets from the luminaire to the grid point: d = sqrt(dx x dx + dy x dy + h
x h) is the slant distance; theta = atan(sqrt(dx x dx + dy x dy) / h) is the vertical angle from nadir; and phi = atan(|dy| /
|dx|) is the horizontal angle, measured from the long axis of the luminaire, which is the +X axis of the coordination
model for every modelled interior luminaire. Where the grid point is directly under the luminaire take phi as zero;
where dx is zero and dy is not, take phi as 90 degrees. The factor (h / d) is the cosine of the angle of incidence, so the
expression is the inverse-square-cosine illuminance in footcandles when I is in candelas and the distances are in feet.
Multiply the sum at each grid point by the light loss factor 0.81 to obtain the direct component of the maintained
illuminance at that point. The average direct component is the arithmetic mean of the direct component over all grid
points.
6. Interreflected component
The interreflected component is uniform over the space and is obtained from the flux that does not reach the work
plane directly, redistributed by the average reflectance of the room surfaces:
    E(indirect) = rho / (1 - rho) x (PHI x LLF - E(direct, average) x A(work plane)) / A(room)
in which PHI is the luminous flux of one luminaire from paragraph 2 multiplied by the number of luminaires in the
space; LLF is 0.81; E(direct, average) is the average direct component of paragraph 5; A(work plane) is the floor area
of the space; and A(room) is the total area of the room surfaces, taken as
    A(room) = 2 x A(floor) + 2 x H x (W + D)
with W and D the room extents and H the finished ceiling height, all from the coordination model. The term in brackets
is taken as zero if it would be negative.

--- Page 3 ---
PCB-01 Rev 1
Harlan Sato Engineers LLC (A/E, Designer of Record)   Page 3
rho is the area-weighted average reflectance of the room surfaces,
    rho = (rho(ceiling) x A(floor) + rho(floor) x A(floor) + rho(wall) x 2 x H x (W + D)) / A(room)
using the ceiling, wall and floor reflectances scheduled for that room on A-601.
7. Reported quantities
The average maintained illuminance of the space is the average direct component plus the interreflected component.
The minimum maintained illuminance is the smallest direct component over the grid plus the interreflected
component. The uniformity is the average maintained illuminance divided by the minimum maintained illuminance.
The lighting power density of the space is the number of luminaires multiplied by the scheduled input watts of the
type, divided by the floor area of the space. The whole-building interior lighting power density is the total input watts of
all interior luminaires of the building divided by the total interior floor area of all spaces, and is compared with the limit
of IES-26 paragraph 11.7.
8. Re-layout where a quantity is revised
Where the calculation confirms the luminaire quantity shown in the coordination model, the luminaire positions of the
model govern and are used as they are.
Where a different quantity n is evaluated for a space, do not attempt to preserve the modelled positions: lay the n
luminaires out again on a uniform grid over the whole space, by the following rule. Take the number of columns
(along the X axis of the space) as the nearest whole number to sqrt(n x W / D), not less than one and not more than
n, in which W and D are the room extents along X and Y. Take the number of rows as n divided by the number of
columns, rounded up to a whole number. Place the luminaires at the centres of the cells of that row-by-column grid:
the luminaire in row r and column c, counting r and c from zero, is at
    x = X(origin) + W x (c + 0.5) / columns,  y = Y(origin) + D x (r + 0.5) / rows
filling row by row, and keep the first n positions so generated. The mounting height is unchanged. This rule is used for
every space and every quantity so that two engineers evaluating the same quantity obtain the same layout.
9. Data sources
Candela tables: the LM-63 file named for each type on E-501. Input watts, type marks and descriptions: E-501.
Surface reflectances: A-601. Room extents, ceiling heights, luminaire quantities, luminaire positions and luminaire
mounting heights: the coordination model 50_bim/BLDG4410-E_RevC.ifc. Illuminance targets and uniformity limits:
IES-26 paragraph 11.6. Lighting power density limit: IES-26 paragraph 11.7. Light loss factor, grid spacing, uniformity
definition and margin of error: Section 26 51 00 and this memorandum.

impedance and X/R; cables from the conductor data sheet CDS-7 (copper, steel conduit), one-way routed length from
the electrical coordination model, divided by the number of parallel sets; dry-type transformers from Table 1. Refer
impedances to the faulted bus voltage by the square of the voltage ratio.

(kA symmetrical): 480 V equipment 14, 18, 22, 25, 35, 42, 50, 65, 85, 100; 208 V equipment 10, 22, 25, 42, 65. Do
not specify below the UFC 3-520-01 minimum interrupting ratings. Series ratings are not permitted.

Add 4 times the full-load amperes of the motors connected at a 480 V bus, arithmetically, at that bus and at every 480
V bus upstream of it. Motor loads at 208 V are neglected. The generator is not a fault source for this evaluation (utility
source governs).

import re
from collections import Counter
base = '/filesystem/final_batch4__electrical_task8_electrical_specs__blind'

    lines = f.read().splitlines()

    m = re.match(r'^#(\d+)=([A-Z0-9_]+)\((.*)\);$', line)
    if m:
        types[m.group(2)] += 1
for k, v in sorted(types.items()):
    print(f'{k}: {v}')
"

In addition to NFPA 70 requirements, facilities located outside of the United States must 
also comply with the applicable host nation standards.  Host nation voltage and

GENERAL BUILDING REQUIREMENTS. 
Comply with UFC 1-200-01, DoD Building Code. UFC 1-200-01 provides applicability of 
model building codes and government unique criteria for typical design disciplines and 
building systems, as well as for accessibility, antiterrorism, security, high performance 
and sustainability requirements, and safety. Use this UFC in addition to UFC 1-200-01 
and the UFCs and government criteria referenced therein.

All facility-related control systems (including systems separate from a utility monitoring 
and control system) must be planned, designed, acquired, executed, and maintained in 
accordance with UFC 4-010-06, and as required by individual Service Implementation 
Policy. 
Cybersecurity is implemented to mitigate vulnerabilities to all DoD real property facility-
related control systems to a level that is acceptable to the System Owner and 
Authorizing Official.  UFC 4-010-06 provides requirements for integrating cybersecurity 
into the design and construction of control systems.

National Electrical Code, and the requirements herein.  Electrical safety requirements,

operation of electrical systems are provided in UFC 3-560-01.

Criteria that are more stringent than NFPA 70 requirements take precedence over 
NFPA requirements. This UFC does not address COPS requirements.

CHAPTER 3 POWER DISTRIBUTION AND UTILIZATION 
3-1 
TRANSFORMERS. 
The transformer design criteria provided herein apply to interior applications and to dry-
type transformers fed by distribution traditionally placed in/for the facility downstream of 
the main service.  Most facilities will be supplied by an exterior utility system pad-
mounted transformer.  
Interior transformers shall be sized according to the NEC. 
3-1.1 
Low Voltage Transformers. 
Specify dry-type transformers in accordance with NEMA ST 20 and the following: 
• 
For transformers rated for 15 kVA or larger, use transformers with a 428 
degrees F (220 degree C) insulation system not to exceed a 239 degrees 
F (115 degree C) rise capable of carrying continuously 115 percent of 
nameplate kVA without exceeding insulation rating at a maximum ambient 
temperature of 104 degrees F (40 degrees C).  Provide a transformer of 
80 degrees C temperature rise capable of carrying continuously 130 
percent of nameplate kVA without exceeding insulation rating when 
additional overload capacity is required. 
• 
Transformers rated less than 15 kVA can use a 356 degrees F (180 
degree C) insulation system not to exceed an 176 degrees F (80 degree 
C) rise at a maximum ambient temperature of 104 degrees F (40 degrees 
C). 
• 
When the transformer is located in areas where noise is a factor, specify 
sound levels at least 3 decibels below recommended values established 
by NEMA ST 20.   
• 
Derate the transformer in accordance with the manufacturer’s guidance for 
locations with a maximum ambient temperature above 104 degrees F (40 
degrees C) and in accordance NEMA ST 20 for altitudes higher than 
3,300 feet (1,000 meters). 
Include the following as part of the installation: 
• 
Design system such that transformer vibrations are not transmitted to the 
surrounding structure.  Small transformers can usually be solidly mounted 
on a reinforced concrete floor or wall.  Flexible mounting will be necessary 
if the transformer is mounted to the structure in a normally low-ambient 
noise area. 
• 
Use flexible couplings and conduit to minimize vibration transmission 
through the connection points. 

=== UFC 3-520-01 Page 18 ===
UFC 3-520-01 
16 January 2025 
Change 1, 21 January 2026

• 
Locate the transformer in spaces where the sound level is not increased 
by sound reflection.  For example, in terms of sound emission, the least 
desirable transformer location is in a corner near the ceiling because the 
walls and ceiling function as a megaphone. 
• 
Provide adequate ventilation in transformer spaces to prevent the 
temperature rise from exceeding the transformer rating. 
Refer to TSEWG TP-05, Interior Transformer Ratings and Installation, at 
https://wbdg.org/dod/supp-tech-documents for additional information regarding 
transformers and transformer ratings. 
3-1.2 
Other Transformer Types. 
Do not use unless justified and documented in the design analysis.  Refer to Appendix 
B for additional guidance for applications involving significant harmonic distortion. 
3-2 
SERVICE ENTRANCE AND DISTRIBUTION EQUIPMENT. 
Locate service entrance equipment and other major electrical equipment in a dedicated 
electrical space. Provide a main breaker on each service entrance either outside of a 
building or structure or inside nearest the point of entrance of the service conductors in 
accordance with NFPA 70. Service feeders may be installed under the building only 
when necessary or for optimal routing.  Distances shall be minimal.  Locate other 
electrical equipment, such as electrical panels, in dedicated spaces. 
Note:  Identify when 100 percent rated circuit breakers are included in the design. 
Size circuit breaker interrupting ratings based on the available short circuit current; 
however, do not select circuit breakers less than 10 kA symmetrical interrupting rating 
for voltages 240V and below and 14 kA symmetrical interrupting rating for 480V 
applications.  The use of series-rated combinations of breakers to clear a fault that 
utilize an individual breaker rated at less than the available fault current is prohibited. 
Do not use fusible overcurrent devices except when non-fusible overcurrent devices will 
not comply with NFPA 70 requirements for selective coordination. 
3-2.1 
Spare Capacity. 
Provide a minimum of 15% empty space and 15% spare capacity (ampacity) for all 
switchgear, switchboards, panelboards, and load centers. For flush-mounted 
equipment, provide spare conduits extending up above the ceiling and down below 
raised floors when applicable.  For panelboards, provide one spare conduit, minimum of 
¾-inch (20 mm), for every three spare circuit breakers and for every three empty pole 
positions. Round up the sum of spare breakers and empty pole positions to the nearest 
multiple of three.

Note:  Do not use spare capacity as part of the demand calculations specified in UFC 
3-501-01.  The overall calculations already account for this spare capacity with the 15% 
allowance for future load growth specified in UFC 3-501-01 load analysis calculations

3-2.2

CHAPTER 1:  GENERAL REQUIREMENTS 
1.2 
 
 
 
 
1.1 
GENERAL 
This manual is a guide for Architects, Engineers and Lighting Design Professionals 
(hereafter referred as A/E) for the planning and design of the lighting and lighting 
control systems (hereafter referred to as lighting systems, or systems) at the 
Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) facilities. 
VA requires A/E to read, understand, and use this manual in the planning and design of 
the systems in all VA construction projects – minor, major and non-recurring-
maintenance (NRM).  A/E - who provide planning and design of the systems - shall be 
licensed professionals who have engaged mainly in the specialized profession of 
lighting system design and all related duties of lighting system design. 
Lighting systems are dependent on electrical power for their function and operation. 
Therefore, this manual shall be used in conjunction with the VA Electrical Design 
Manual (EDM) to produce complete and functional systems. 
VA expects that the systems planned and designed with the use of this manual shall 
meet their primary objectives stated in Chapter 2.  In order to provide the latitude 
needed to incorporate new technologies and concepts, or to accommodate adverse 
existing conditions, technical deviations from the stipulations of this manual may be 
made.  Deviations may be made only if a safe, reliable, functional and energy-efficient 
design shall result.  Such deviations must be approved by VA’s Project Team which 
consists of Contracting Officer (CO), Project Manager (PM), Contracting Officer 
Representative (COR), and Authority Having Jurisdiction (AHJ).  Deviations are not 
permitted from those requirements included in shall comply with all public laws, federal 
regulations, executive orders, and applicable codes.  
 
Request for deviations shall be submitted in writing by A/E to CO and AHJ through PM 
or COR.  At the minimum, request for deviations shall contain the following elements:  
• 
Narrative detailing reasons for the deviations. 
• 
Narrative detailing the design and technical information relating to the deviations. 
• 
Design drawings of the deviations (if applicable). 
• 
Lighting and engineering calculations (if applicable). 
• 
Estimate of cost impact caused by the deviations. 
• 
Estimate of schedule impact caused by the deviations. 
• 
Supporting documents such as existing site survey photographs, drawings and 
documents (if applicable). 
 
Request for deviations shall be considered approved only after A/E has received a 
written approval with signature from CO, and AHJ. 
 
1.2 
RESPONSIBILITY 
A/E shall provide all necessary professional services to perform planning and design of 
the systems for the project.  A/E shall be responsible and liable for the planning and 
design in accordance with the contract, professional engineering and design practices, 
latest VA standards and applicable codes, and project-specific requirements. 
 

=== VA Lighting Manual Page 8 ===
CHAPTER 1:  GENERAL REQUIREMENTS 
1.3 
 
 
 
 
1.3 
AUTHORITY HAVING JURISDICTION (AHJ) 
Authority Having Jurisdiction (AHJ) for VHA is the Deputy Undersecretary for 
Operations and Management (DUSHOM), or his/her designee.  Due to the nature of 
change in personnel and contact information in VA, AHJ and his/her contact information 
may not be constant.  Therefore, A/E shall obtain AHJ’s name and contact information 
from CO, PM or COR. 
1.4 
COORDINATION 
1.4.1 PLANNING AND DESIGN 
A/E shall coordinate planning and design of the lighting systems with architectural, 
electrical, structural, civil, site utility and site work, HVAC, plumbing, fire 
protection/alarm systems, and sustainable designs, as applicable. A/E shall coordinate 
design information between construction drawings to ensure clarity, completeness and 
correctness in accordance with latest VA Standards and applicable codes, project-
specific requirements, and pre-existing conditions (if any). 
A/E shall coordinate and edit applicable VA master specifications, and standard details 
to ensure clarity, completeness and correctness in accordance with latest VA 
Standards and applicable codes, project-specific requirements, and pre-existing 
conditions (if any). 
For renovation projects, A/E shall perform site visit(s) to investigate, and document pre-
existing conditions. Findings of pre-existing conditions shall be taken into account for 
the planning and design of the project. 
For exterior spaces, focus should be on coordination of hardscape, softscape, and 
landscape. Base designs for pole-mounted luminaires should be coordinated with civil 
and structural engineers. A/E shall reference VA base-mounting details and modify to 
meet specific project scope.  Base-mounting details shall be shown on drawings. 
For interior spaces, focus should be on coordination of luminaire type, trim and layout 
with ceiling type, construction, layout, plenum depths, diffusers, ceiling tracks, and all 
ceiling-mounted objects. Luminaire layout should be coordinated with furniture, 
casework, millwork, and equipment layouts. Lighting control device locations should be 
coordinated with interior features and furnishings to assure ready access, as well as 
proper sensor performance. 
1.4.2 INSTALLATION 
A/E is not responsible to provide (furnish, install, and connect) lighting systems. 
However, lighting design document shall show clear, complete and correct 
information regarding all aspects of lighting and electrical power designs. 
During the submittal review phase, A/E shall coordinate lighting equipment submittals 
with ceiling system submittals to ensure complete and correct coordination between 
lighting and ceiling systems.

1.6 
DAYLIGHTING 
1.6.1 GENERAL 
A/E shall strive to employ daylighting practice in the design. When appropriate, lighting 
control strategies should integrate daylighting and artificial lighting. 
Location of windows and skylights in a building must be designed to avoid the 
admittance of direct sun on task surfaces or occupants. Suitable glare control devices 
such as blinds or shades should be incorporated into the design. 
Daylight harvesting controls must be commissioned. The system must have the lighting 
set points properly configured if the system is to properly respond to available daylight. 
The success of a daylighting design depends on commissioning and occupant 
education and training. 
 
1.7 
ABBREVIATIONS 
Use only the abbreviations and symbols shown in the VA Standard Details (PG-18-4) 
and the Uniform Drawing System (UDS) of the U.S. National CAD Standard (NCS). A 
complete listing of terms and abbreviations can be found on the Construction 
Specification Institute (CSI) website under Standards and Formats. 
 
 
 
 
 
 

=== VA Lighting Manual Page 11 ===
CHAPTER 1:  GENERAL REQUIREMENTS 
1.6 
 
 
 
 
1.8 
GLOSSARY 
Ambient Lighting – Lighting throughout an area that produces general illumination. 
Area Lighting Luminaire – A complete lighting device consisting of a light source and 
ballast, where appropriate, together with its direct appurtenances such as globe, 
reflector, refractor, housing, and such support as is integral with the housing. The pole, 
post, or bracket is not considered part of the luminaire. 
Average Luminance – Luminance is a property of a geometric ray. Luminance as 
measured by conventional meters is averaged with respect to two independent 
variables, area and solid angle; both must be defined for a complete description of a 
luminance measurement. 
BAS – Building automation system. 
Baffle – A single opaque or translucent element to shield a source from direct view at 
certain angles, to absorb or block unwanted light, or to reflect and redirect light. 
Ballast – A device used with an electric-discharge lamp to obtain the necessary circuit 
conditions (voltage, current, and waveform) for starting and operating. 
Ballast Factor – The fractional flux of a fluorescent lamp operated on a ballast 
compared to the flux when operated on the standard (reference) ballast specified for 
rating lamp lumens. 
Bollard – Luminaires having the appearance of a short, thick post, used for walkway 
and grounds lighting.  The optical components are usually top-mounted. 
Bowl – An open-top diffusing glass or plastic enclosure used to shield a light source 
from direct view and to redirect or scatter the light. 
Bracket (mast arm) – An attachment to a lamp post or pole from which a luminaire is 
suspended. 
Candela, cd – The SI unit of luminous intensity, equal to one lumen per steradian 
(lm/sr). 
Candlepower (cp), I = dφ/dω – Luminous intensity expressed in candelas. 
Coefficient of Utilization (CU) – The ratio of luminous flux (lumens) calculated as 
received on the work plane to the total luminous flux (lumens) emitted by the lamps 
alone.  It is equal to the product of room utilization factor and luminaire efficiency. 
Color Matching – the action of making a color appear the same as a given color. 
Color Rendering – a general expression for the effect of a light source on the color 
appearance of objects in conscious or subconscious comparison with their color 
appearance under a reference light source. 
 
 
 
 

=== VA Lighting Manual Page 12 ===
CHAPTER 1:  GENERAL REQUIREMENTS 
1.7 
 
 
 
 
Color Rendering Index (of a light source) (CRI) – a measure of the degree of color 
shift objects undergo when illuminated by the light source as compared with those 
same objects when illuminated by a reference source of comparable color temperature. 
Color Temperature (of a light source) – the absolute temperature of a blackbody 
radiator having a chromaticity equal to that of the light source. See Correlated Color 
Temperature. 
Contrast – See Luminance Contrast. 
Correlated Color Temperature (of a light source) (CCT) – The absolute temperature 
of a blackbody whose chromaticity most nearly resembles that of the light source. 
 
Daylight Availability – The luminous flux from the sun plus sky at a specific location, 
time, date, and sky condition. 
Diffused Lighting – Lighting provided on the work plane or on an object that is not 
incident predominantly from any particular direction. 
Dimmer – A device used to control the intensity of light emitted by a luminaire by 
controlling the voltage or current available to it. 
Direct Glare – Glare resulting from high luminance or insufficiently shielded light 
sources in the field of view. It is usually associated with bright areas, such as 
luminaires, ceilings, and windows that are outside the visual task or region being 
viewed.  A direct glare source can also affect performance by distracting attention. 
Direct-Indirect Lighting – A variant of general diffuse lighting in which the luminaires 
emit little or no light at angles near the horizontal. 
Direct Lighting – Lighting involves luminaires that distribute 90% to 100% of the 
emitted light in the general direction of the surface to be illuminated. The term usually 
refers to light emitted in a downward direction. 
Directional Lighting – Lighting provided on the work plane or on an object. Light that 
is predominantly from a preferred direction. 
Disability Glare – The effect of stray light in the eye whereby visibility and visual 
performance are reduced. A direct glare source that produces discomfort can also 
produce disability glare by introducing a measurable amount of stray light in the eye. 
Discomfort Glare – Glare that produces discomfort. It does not necessarily interfere 
with visual performance or visibility. 
Downlight – A small direct lighting unit that directs the light downward and can be 
recessed, surface-mounted, or suspended. 
 
 
 
 
 

=== VA Lighting Manual Page 13 ===
CHAPTER 1:  GENERAL REQUIREMENTS 
1.8 
 
 
 
 
Efficacy – See Luminous Efficacy of a Source of Light. 
Efficiency – See Luminaire Efficiency. 
Electroluminescence – The emission of light from a phosphor excited by an 
electromagnetic field. 
Emergency Exit – A way out of the premises that is intended to be used only during an 
emergency. 
Emergency Egress Lighting – Lighting designed to supply illumination essential to the 
safety of life and property in the event of a failure of the normal supply. The system 
must be capable of providing minimum required illuminance specified in NFPA 101, 
Code for Safety to Life from Fire in Buildings and Structures, Section 5.9.

1 
CHAPTER 1 INTRODUCTION 
1-1 
BACKGROUND. 
Unified Facilities Guide Specifications (UFGS) are the set of standardized, 
comprehensive specifications used by the DoD for designing and constructing facilities.   
These specifications provide common requirements across DoD for safety, 
sustainability, durability, and functionality and reference applicable consensus building 
codes, DoD-defined requirements, and statutory and regulatory requirements.  UFGS 
ensure consistency, quality, and efficiency across various projects by providing a 
standardized framework for a project team to use and edit for their project.  These 
specifications help streamline the specification process, reduce errors, and improve 
communication among architects, engineers, contractors, and other stakeholders 
involved in design and construction projects. 
1-2 
REISSUES AND CANCELS. 
This UFS reissues and cancels UFC 1-300-02, Unified Facilities Guide Specifications 
(UFGS) Format Standard, dated 1 April 2014 with Changes 1-3. 
1-3 
PURPOSE AND SCOPE. 
This UFS provides guidance for the preparation of UFGS and establishes the general 
content and format of UFGS and project specifications.  Each DWG is responsible for 
the technical content, format, and overall quality of their UFGS.  Publication of UFGS is 
available by electronic media, not proprietary, and at no cost to the user. 
Preparers for both UFGS Masters and project specifications must use this UFS.  
Specific guidance for each is provided as applicable. 
1-4 
APPLICABILITY. 
This UFS follows the same applicability as UFC 1-200-01, paragraph 1.3 with no 
exceptions, applying to all the government elements and contractors preparing UFGS 
for DoD-owned Facilities. 
1-5 
REFERENCES. 
APPENDIX B contains a list of references used in this document.  The publication date 
of the code or standard is not included in this document.  Unless otherwise specified, 
the most recent edition of the referenced publication applies.

CHAPTER 2 UFGS REQUIREMENTS 
2-1 
UFGS SECTION ORGANIZATION. 
This paragraph describes the organization of a UFGS section. 
2-1.1 
Construction Specifications Institute (CSI). 
CSI prescribes the use of three parts in each section and a consistent subject matter 
sequence within each part.  These recommendations are included in Appendix A and 
must be followed to the extent practical in UFGS.  When a part has no content, insert 
"Not used." in the body of the text. 
2-1.2 
Table of Contents (TOC). 
SpecsIntact has two options for printing the Table of Contents using the Print/Publish 
function:  1) For the entire project or master, and 2) For the section.  The Project or 
Master TOC is printed as a separate document.  The Section TOC is printed within the 
section when the Combine Sections and Section TOC is selected.  For instructions, 
refer to the SpecsIntact eLearning modules found in Chapter 4: Process and 
Print/Publish on the SpecsIntact website 
(https://www.wbdg.org/dod/specsintact/elearning).

2-4 
WRITING STYLE. 
Write in a direct, active voice with simple, concise sentences.  Avoid ambiguous, 
indefinite terms such as "too short" or "relatively simple."  Define what applies instead of 
using "applicable" or other indefinite wording.  Do not use "as shown on the drawings" 
as this phrase is frequently overlooked.  If used in a UFGS and the item is not shown on 
the drawings, then the item is not specified.  For additional guidance, see the Federal 
Plain Language Guidelines (https://www.plainlanguage.gov/guidelines/). 
2-4.1 
Mood, Tense, and Voice. 
Use the imperative mood (such as, Install equipment) except when clarity requires the 
use of the indicative mood (such as, Equipment must). 
Speak only to the Contractor, not the subcontractor, supplier, or manufacturer.  
Directing the Contractor through these parties can be misinterpreted as indicating 
responsibility.  Stating "the manufacturer must provide," could be incorrectly interpreted 
as informing the Contractor that a party other than the Contractor is responsible.  It is 
unnecessary to differentiate between the Contractor’s actions and the Contractor's 
various suppliers, as this could be interpreted as assigning work.  Do not use the 
specification to instruct the Contracting Officer. 
2-4.2 
Abbreviations and Acronyms. 
Use of abbreviations and acronyms must follow the practices within the discipline 
involved.  At the first use, write out the term completely and follow with the abbreviation 
or acronym in parentheses.  Use abbreviations for units such as psi, cfm, and kW, and 
be consistent in their use. 
2-4.3 
Units. 
Spell out numbers zero - nine, except units of time and measurement, and use 
numerals for numbers 10 and above.  Avoid starting a sentence with a number, but 
when unavoidable, always spell out the number when it is the first word of a sentence.    
Do not repeat a spelled-out number with a numeral in parentheses.

2-4.4 
Terminology. 
• 
The use of “shall” is prohibited.  “Shall” imposes an obligation to act but 
may be confused with prediction of future action. 
• 
Avoid the use of "must".  If use cannot be avoided, use “must” to prescribe 
mandatory requirements, actions, and procedures.  “Must” imposes 
obligation and indicates a necessity to act. 
• 
Do not use the word "should" in the specification text for mandatory 
requirements as "should" implies a recommendation.  "Should" may be in 
designer notes to indicate desirable procedures that are advisory in 
nature. 
• 
Do not use “Contractor must provide”, use “Provide”.  Project 
specifications are already directed to the Contractor, who is responsible 
for performing the work as shown and specified. 
• 
Do not use the term "furnish" unless only delivery of material to the site is 
required.  Similarly, do not use the term “install’ unless the Government or 
others will furnish equipment or materials and Contractor will install.  Use 
"provide" to mean "furnish and install". 
• 
Do not use “to be” for describing work that will be accomplished by the 
Contractor.  “To be” implies that someone will accomplish the work other 
than the Contractor, such as the Government or another Contractor. 
• 
Do not use “proposed”, as it can be interpreted to mean future work by 
others or work not in this Contract.  If work will be accomplished by the 
Government, for example, say “Government will remove storage building 
prior to start of construction”. 
• 
Do not use the word "per", use "in accordance with". 
• 
Avoid the use of colloquial terms or jargon.  For example, do not use 
"deck" for floor, or "head" for toilet. 
• 
Eliminate redundant wording such as "conforming to", "all", and "type".  
For example, when stating “paint doors”, all doors are implied. 
• 
Do not use indefinite items such as "etc.", "any”, and "and/or". 
• 
Do not use vague words and phrases or escape clauses such as "in this 
specification", "as may be required", "as necessary", "an approved type", 
"as approved/directed/determined by the Contracting Officer", "first class 
workmanship", "securely", "thoroughly", "suitable", "properly", "good 
working order", "neatly", "carefully", and "installed in a neat and 
workmanlike manner".

CHAPTER 1  INTRODUCTION 
1-1 
PURPOSE AND SCOPE. 
The purpose of this UFC is to provide technical requirements for general aspects of the 
electrical design of projects. Apply the criteria provided in this UFC for the development 
of the plans, specifications, calculations, and Design/Build Request for Proposals 
(RFP). It serves as the minimum electrical design requirements for design-build and 
design-bid-build projects. Project conditions may dictate the need for a design that 
exceeds these minimum requirements. 
1-1.1 
UFC Hierarchy. 
This UFC provides the top-tier baseline requirements for electrical UFCs and is 
intended as a reference for all electrical work on projects.  All electrical UFCs listed in 
Appendix E rely on this UFC for overall requirements regarding design analysis and 
documentation. 
1-1.2 
Upgrades and Modifications to Existing Systems. 
Modernization of electrical systems solely for the purpose of meeting design criteria in 
UFCs is not required. Upgrades or modifications to electrical systems should consider 
the design criteria in this UFC, but it is not intended that an entire facility or system 
require modernization solely because of a minor modification. 
For minor projects, determine if the project will affect existing electrical system 
calculations such as by modifying circuit breaker settings. If any electrical system 
calculations are affected by the modification, update the calculations, including the arc 
flash calculation, as part of the project. 
Note: Arc flash calculation updates are necessary for electrical safety. 
1-2 
REISSUES AND CANCELS. 
This UFC reissues and cancels UFC 3-501-01, Electrical Engineering, dated 06 October 
2015. 
1-3 
APPLICABILITY. 
This UFC applies to the planning, design, construction, sustainment, restoration, and 
modernization of DoD-owned facilities.  It is applicable to all methods of project delivery 
and levels of construction as defined by UFC 1-200-01 section 1-3. 
1-4

g. 
For new low voltage systems, an upstream circuit breaker can be credited 
to clear the arcing fault if the circuit breaker commissioning process

h. 
Calculated energy in cal/cm2 at each evaluated location. The design goal 
is to establish arc flash levels that result in 8 cal/cm2 or less. Consider 
remote racking mechanisms to rack breakers in and out to limit personnel 
exposure to an arc flash event. Specifically identify locations where this 
energy level cannot be achieved, such as upstream of a main breaker 
(between the breaker and an upstream transformer) or downstream of 
UPS systems. 
i.
